title: Types of RNN | Many to Many | One to Many | Many to One RNNs
full_text: Hi guys, my name is Nitesh and you are  welcome to CampusX. In this video, we  will continue our deep learning  playlist. So, we are currently studying  RNNs, and we have understood the RNN  architecture so far and have also  implemented it in Keras. And moving  forward, my plan is to teach  backpropagation. But before that, we  will cover one topic today, and that is  the types of RNNs. Okay? So, you should  know what the different architectures  of RNNs are, and then, based on that,  we will study backpropagation further.  Okay? So, this is a short video. It's a  nice video, but do watch it because it  will be useful later. Okay? Let's start  the video. So guys, before starting the  video, let's discuss once what we have  studied in RNNs so far. Okay? So, in  the first video of RNNs, I gave you a  roadmap. A roadmap, or you can call it  an overview, of what RNNs are. What are  their applications? I told you all this  in the first video. After that, in the  second video, we started studying RNNs  at a theoretical level. Okay? Where we  discussed what the RNN architecture  looks like. How the weights are in RNNs . Then in the third video, we  practically implemented RNNs in Keras.  Okay? On a problem called sentiment  analysis. Right? Now, what is our plan  going forward? That we have to learn  how the backpropagation algorithm works  in the case of RNNs. Okay? But before  studying backpropagation, I would like  to talk about a topic which is  important, and that is what the  different types of RNN architectures  are. It is important to study this  topic. Why? Because depending on the  type of RNN, the backpropagation  algorithm varies a little bit. So I  thought I would tell you once what the  various types of RNN architectures are,  and then when we study backpropagation,  we will cover how backpropagation is  applied in different types of RNNs.  Okay? So, I will tell you one thing  beforehand: there are four types of RNN  architectures. The first one is  Many-to-One. Okay? After that comes  One-to-Many. After that comes  Many-to-Many. And the last one is  One-to-One. Now, our goal for this  video is to discuss these four  architectures or four types in detail.  And not only that, I will provide you  with examples of all of them. That will  give you clarity on which type of RNN  you should use for what kind of  application. Okay? So, let's start with  many-to-one. So, many-to-one is an RNN  architecture that you might already  understand from the name itself. It  expects a sequence as an input. Okay? A  sequence can mean anything. It could be  a sentence, characters, or it could be  time-series data. Okay? But it must be  a sequence. And in the output, it gives  you a non-sequence output or  non-sequential output. Okay? One  example could be integers or numbers,  or in more technical terms, you could  call them scalars. Okay? Like one or  zero, depending on the classes. So, let  me tell you what kind of applications  this architecture is used for. One  example could be sentiment analysis. We  just studied that as well. So, in  sentiment analysis, you receive text as  input, and after processing that text  word by word, you have to determine the  sentiment of that text, one or zero.  Okay? So you can see here that the  input is a sequence of data. In this  case, it is words. And the output is  basically a scalar, one or zero. Okay?  Another example that falls under this  type of application is rating  prediction. Right? Suppose you are  building an application where you have  movie reviews. And by reading the  review, you want to provide a star  prediction, as in a star rating, of how  the user rated that movie. Okay?  Between one and five. Again, the input  is textual, which means it is a  sequence, but the output is a number  between one and five, or one star, two  stars, three stars; it could also act  as a multi-class classification problem . Okay? So these are some examples  where you use many-to-one RNN. Okay?  Now I will show you what a many-to-one  RNN looks like. The good thing is that  you have already seen many-to-one RNN.  Everything we have studied in this  course so far has actually been on  many-to-one RNN. Okay? A many-to-one  architecture looks like this. You send  your input from here. From here, you  get the input of the previous time step . All right? And here your activation  function is applied, and from here you  get the current time step's output, and  at the last time step, you calculate  the output. So, this is the compact  representation. If I show you this  unfolded over several time steps, it  will look something like this, where  you sent the first word from here. From  here, you are receiving an input of  zero. From here, you calculated O1,  which is being fed back to the same  place. And from here, you sent the next  word. From here, O2 is being calculated . From here, you sent the third word.  From here, O3 is being calculated. And  so on. And in the last step, as soon as  you sent the last word. Now from here,  your y-hat, as in your main prediction,  is being made—whether it will be one  or zero. This is the same thing we have  studied so far, and these blocks you  see are your recurrent blocks. And this  is basically a simple RNN. These are  simple RNN blocks. All right? So, this  was an example of a many-to-one  architecture. Yes, looking at this  architecture, you must be understanding  why it is called many-to-one. Because  you can clearly see you are providing  multiple inputs. But you are getting  only one thing in the output. That is  why we call this a many-to-one  architecture. All right? The next RNN  architecture we have is one-to-many.  Again, from the name, you might be  understanding how this will operate.  This is an RNN architecture where you  get normal non-sequential data as input . All right? It could be anything that  is non-sequential, which has no  sequence. It could be numbers or it  could be an image. Even an image is  your non-sequential data. Because at  the end, it is just a matrix of numbers . All right? But the output you get  here is sequential. Like words,  sentences, time series, it could be  anything. All right? If you talk about  the architecture, its architecture is  the exact opposite of our previous type . I will show you what happens here,  that again you have RNN blocks. Like a  simple RNN block. And you provide your  input there. Since the input is a  single one, you provide the input only  once. All right? And then what happens?  From this input, at every time step,  you get an output. And you send that  output to the next time step as well.  You get an output there too. And this  continues like this. Okay? Like this.  This is the architecture. So you can  see it's called one-to-many because you  provide input once, but you get  multiple outputs. There are many  outputs. Okay? Now I know you might be  wondering, what kind of application  could this architecture be useful for?  So, I will give you an example that is  actually used in the industry. So there  is this application called image  captioning. In image captioning, you  feed an image into your neural network,  which is non-sequential data, and your  goal is for the neural network to give  you a textual representation of what is  inside that image. Okay? Let me explain  this with an example. Suppose you  provide an image where a guy is playing  cricket. Okay? So as soon as you feed  this into your neural network, your  neural network will give you this  output: a man is playing cricket. So  you can see your input is a  non-sequential image, and in the output , you are getting sequential data. So  this is one application where this  architecture is used a lot. There are  many more applications, such as another  application: music generation. Okay?  Where you pass a single thing as input,  and music notes are constantly being  generated there. Okay? So this is the  second type of RNN architecture. The  next RNN type is, in my opinion, the  most interesting one. And it is called  many-to-many RNN. Okay? Can you  understand from the name? A  many-to-many RNN is an RNN type where  you get sequential data in the input  and you provide sequential data in the  output as well. Okay? And because of  this, it is often called a  sequence-to-sequence model. And we are  going to work a lot on this in the  future. Okay? So sequence-to-sequence  models or many-to-many RNNs are such  RNN architectures where you get  sequential data as input and you  provide sequential data as output. Okay ? Now, there are two types of this. The  first type is same-length many-to-many.  And the second is variable-length  many-to-many. I am explaining the  difference between the two to you. Same  length happens when your input sequence  size is the same as your output  sequence size. All right? One example  could be part-of-speech tagging. So, if  you have studied a little bit of NLP,  it is a very, very popular task in NLP.  Where what you do is, you have an input  sentence. Let's say, "My name is Nitish ." And what you have to do is, in the  pre-processing stage, find the  part-of-speech of every word. Because  apparently, it will help you later on.  Like, this is a pronoun. This is a noun . This is a helping verb. And this is a  noun. All right? So you can see, what  are you doing in the input? You are  giving four words. And for every word,  you are also getting an output. So this  is an application where as many inputs  as you provide, you will get the same  number of outputs. All right? Another  example of this type of application  could be Named Entity Recognition.  Again, a very popular task where for  every word you decide whether it is an  entity or not. All right? Like, "Let's  meet at 7 PM""at the airport." All  right? And you have to figure out which  of these are entities that you need to  work on in the future. So for every  input, for every word, you will assign  a number, one or zero; for example, 7  PM could be an entity, airport could be  an entity. So generally, this thing  comes in very handy when building  chatbots and such. So these are both  applications of the same length type.  And if you talk about it  architecturally, how the architecture  of a same-length many-to-many RNN looks , I will quickly draw and show you. So  what happens is that you have the same  RNN or a simple RNN module. You send  your inputs there, and for every time  step, you also get an output. And you  send that output to the next time step.  Where you provide the next input as  well, and then calculate the next  output. And this goes on until the  number of inputs are exhausted. All  right? So this is the flow diagram of a  same-length many-to-many RNN. All right ? So I told you that there are two  types. So we have discussed the first  type, the same-length one. Now let me  show you what a variable-length  many-to-many RNN is and how it works.  So first, let me tell you again an  application of a variable-length one. A  very good example of variable-length is  machine translation. All right? Machine  translation means an application where  you translate a sentence from one  language into a second language. You  have probably used this in Google  Translate as well. Right? Google  Translate internally uses this type of  RNN model. Right? So why is it variable  length? Let's try to understand that.  Right? I don't have an exact example  coming to mind at this moment. But I  will still try to explain it to you.  Let's say I said, "Hi, my name is  Nitish." Right? This is our input in  English, and let's say we have to  translate it into Hindi. And let's say  the translation in Hindi is: "Mera naam  Nitish hai." Right? Now, this is an  example where the number of words in  your English input is the same as the  words in your Hindi output. But I guess  you can understand that you cannot  guarantee that the number of words in  the input will be the same as the  output language. It is possible that  some languages represent sentences very  efficiently in fewer words, while some  languages might not be as efficient and  take more words. So, machine  translation is a very good example of a  variable-length many-to-many RNN. Right ? If you talk from an architectural  point of view, the architecture of such  an application looks something like  this. So, what do you do in the  beginning? You first provide your  entire input. For example, if I had  four words here, what would I do? I  would input all four first, like this.  At every time step, I am providing my  input like this. Right? Now, once I  have provided the last word as input,  the translation actually starts from  there, and here I get my y1. Then y2.  Then y3, and so on, for however many  words are coming in the output. So, I  guess the question might be arising in  your mind: why did we follow this  architecture where we waited to see the  entire input before giving a single  output? I guess if you try to  understand it logically, you will  realize that translation is a task  where you don't translate on a  word-by-word level. Right? You always  read the whole sentence to perform a  translation. You read its meaning,  understand the grammar, and only then  do you decide what its translation  should be in another language. You  don't just read the first word and  translate it. Read the second word and  translated it. Read the third and  translated it. If you do this, you  might lose both the grammatical meaning  and the context. That is why this  architecture first looks at the entire  input and starts generating output only  after you send the last input. Okay? I  hope you are understanding this whole  point. Now, you will see such  architectures referred to as  encoder-decoder models later. So, this  part where you are providing the input  is called the encoder. And the rest,  from where you are extracting the  output, is called the decoder. Okay? In  the future, when we study  sequence-to-sequence models, we will  cover encoder-decoder networks there.  Okay? But I have already given you a  kind of introduction. Okay? Now let's  move on to our last type. That is  one-to-one. The last type of RNN  architecture is one-to-one. Technically  speaking, this is not a type of RNN.  Because if an RNN were one-to-one, it  wouldn't be an RNN at all. If you think  about it. One-to-one means you have an  architecture that expects  non-sequential data as input and  provides non-sequential data as output  as well. Okay? A very simple example of  such an application can be image  classification, where your input data  is an image. It is an image, meaning a  grid of values or a matrix, and your  output is one or zero, whether it is a  cat or not. Okay? So basically,  architecture-wise, it looks like you  are given an input here and you are  generating an output from here. So  basically, there is no recurrence. Okay ? There is no feedback. You are not  talking about any time steps.  Everything is happening in a single  time step. So technically, this is not  an RNN. This is your simple neural  network that you have studied so far.  Your ANN or your CNN. They actually  fall under this. Okay? So I just  mentioned it so you have an  understanding of when things fall under  RNNs and when they do not. Technically  speaking, there are only three types.  Many-to-one, one-to-many, and  many-to-many. And many-to-many has two  types that we just saw. One is same  length and one is variable length. Okay ? So, that is all I wanted to tell you.  This video is short, but it will give  you some perspective on the different  types of architectures. Going forward,  in the next video when we study  backpropagation, I will explain how  backpropagation works for these three  architectures, and then we will  definitely work on many-to-many. Okay?  So, that's it. So, I hope you  understood this entire topic. And if  you liked the video, please like it,  and if you haven't subscribed to the  channel, please subscribe. Okay? See  you in the next video where we will  cover backpropagation. Bye.
